title: The Roman Army: Legions, Auxiliaries and Officers
lead: The Roman army was the real power in AD 69: legions of citizen soldiers, auxiliary cohorts and cavalry wings of non-citizens, commanded by senators and Knights. The New Testament meets its centurions, cohorts and commanders in the Gospels and Acts.

sections.b: Wikipedia describes an imperial legion as about 5,000 men in cohorts and centuries, commanded by a legate (usually a senator), with tribunes and centurions under him, and an eagle carried by the eagle-bearer as its standard. Auxiliaries were non-citizens, in infantry cohorts of about 480 men and in cavalry wings, and Wikipedia says that at the end of a 25-year term the retiring auxiliary and all his children were awarded citizenship, a rule it says is deduced from the date of the first known military diplomas. In Book 1 Tacitus names legions by number and nickname, speaks of cohorts and wings, and shows soldiers taking a personal oath (1:55-57). The Rhine armies were the Upper and the Lower (1:9).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:9; Histories of Tacitus 1:55-57; Histories of Tacitus 1:61

sections.b: A centurion in Capernaum whose slave was ill said, "I am a man placed under someone's authority myself, and I have soldiers under me" (Luke 7:8). Cornelius was "a centurion in the unit called the Italian Cohort" (Acts 10:1). Paul was turned over to "a centurion of the Emperor's Cohort, a man named Julius" (Acts 27:1), and was rescued from a mob by "the commander of the cohort" (Acts 21:31).
